paragraphs.heading: Thirteen days in 1962
paragraphs.text: The Cuban Missile Crisis was a standoff between the United States and the Soviet Union that ran from 16 to 28 October 1962. Many people regard it as the nearest the Cold War ever came to turning into a full nuclear war. At its centre were Soviet nuclear missiles placed on the island of Cuba.

paragraphs.heading: Pressure from Washington
paragraphs.text: The United States had already put nuclear weapons close to the Soviet Union. In 1959 it stationed Thor nuclear missiles in England, a plan called Project Emily, and in 1961 it added Jupiter missiles in Italy and Turkey. Every one of these could reach Moscow. In April 1961 a force of Cuban exiles trained by the US took part in a CIA-led attempt to invade Cuba and topple its government. From November that year the US also ran a violent campaign of terrorism and sabotage on the island, known as the Cuban Project.

paragraphs.heading: Moscow's worries about Cuba
paragraphs.text: Soviet leaders had their own fears too: that Cuba was drifting toward China, with which their relations had grown more and more tense. Toward the end of 1961 Fidel Castro had requested extra SA-2 anti-aircraft missiles, and the Soviets did not act on the request. Meanwhile he accused them of lacking "revolutionary boldness" and opened talks with China about economic aid. In March 1962 he had Anibal Escalante and his pro-Moscow allies pushed out of the Integrated Revolutionary Organizations. This alarmed the Soviet leaders, who sent more SA-2 missiles and a regiment of troops in April. Historian Timothy Naftali argues they saw missile bases as a way to bind Cuba more tightly to the Soviet Union.

paragraphs.heading: Missiles found, a blockade chosen
paragraphs.text: In July 1962 Khrushchev and Castro agreed to base nuclear missiles on Cuba to deter any future US invasion, and work on launch sites began soon after. In October a U-2 spy plane photographed medium- and long-range launch sites. Kennedy gathered the National Security Council and other close advisers into a group called the Executive Committee, or EXCOMM. Some urged an air strike on the missile supplies followed by an invasion, but he picked a gentler path to avoid a declaration of war. On 22 October he ordered a naval blockade to keep more missiles from arriving, and called it a "quarantine" to sidestep what a state of war would formally mean.

paragraphs.heading: The deal
paragraphs.text: In the end Kennedy and Khrushchev reached an agreement. The Soviets would take apart their offensive weapons in Cuba, with the United Nations checking, and in return the US declared publicly that it would not invade Cuba again. In secret, the US also agreed to remove all the offensive weapons it had placed in Turkey. Some Soviet bombers stayed on in Cuba, and the US kept its quarantine until 20 November 1962, when it ended once every offensive missile and bomber had gone. By August 1963 all the Thor missiles in Britain had been stood down.

paragraphs.heading: What came after
paragraphs.text: The crisis made plain that the two powers needed a fast, direct way to talk, and this produced the Moscow–Washington hotline. Later agreements eased US–Soviet tension for several years. The outcome embarrassed Khrushchev, because the removal of US missiles from Italy and Turkey was kept secret, so the Soviets seemed to be backing away from a crisis they had begun. The Soviet ambassador in Washington, Anatoly Dobrynin, said the leadership felt it as "a blow to its prestige bordering on humiliation". Two years later Khrushchev fell from power, partly because the Politburo was embarrassed by his concessions and by his blundering into the crisis.
